# Dispersion Is Residual Biological Variability

For gene $g$ in biological sample $i$, a common RNA-seq model is

$$
Y_{gi}\sim\operatorname{NB}(\mu_{gi},\alpha_g),
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y_{gi}\mid\mathbf x_i)
=\mu_{gi}+\alpha_g\mu_{gi}^2,
$$

with

$$
\log(\mu_{gi})=\log(s_i)+\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta_g.
$$

The offset $s_i$ represents effective library size, the design row $\mathbf x_i$
represents modeled condition, batch, and other covariates, and $\alpha_g\geq0$ is
the gene-specific dispersion. At large means, $\sqrt{\alpha_g}$ is approximately
the residual biological coefficient of variation.

Dispersion is conditional on the fitted mean model. If batch, subject, or another
systematic source is omitted, its variation can be absorbed into $\alpha_g$.
Conversely, an overfitted or aliased design can leave too little information for
estimating residual variation. A dispersion estimate is therefore not an intrinsic
property of a gene: it belongs to a gene, experiment, design, normalization rule,
and probability model together.

The scientific targets are usually expression contrasts in
$\boldsymbol\beta_g$. Dispersion is a nuisance parameter, but a consequential
one: it determines the width of sampling distributions, standard errors, tests,
and intervals. Underestimating it produces overconfident evidence; severe
overestimation sacrifices power.

# Why Gene-wise Estimation Is Unstable

An RNA-seq experiment may measure twenty thousand genes but contain only three or
four independent samples per condition. Each gene has many counts across reads,
yet only the biological samples provide independent information about
sample-to-sample variability. Sequencing deeper primarily reduces the Poisson
component $\mu_{gi}$; it cannot manufacture more realizations of the biological
population.

If $n$ samples are fitted with a design of rank $p$, roughly $n-p$ residual degrees
of freedom inform gene-wise variability. With small $n-p$, an unrestricted
estimate $\widehat\alpha_g$ has high variance. Randomly quiet genes appear nearly
Poisson, while a single unusual observation can make another gene appear highly
dispersed. Plugging either extreme directly into downstream tests makes the
ranking of genes depend too strongly on noise in nuisance estimates.

The parallel structure of genomics offers a remedy. Genes are not biological
replicates, but their estimated dispersions can reveal a shared abundance-dependent
regularity. Modern methods combine gene-specific evidence with this ensemble
pattern. This is information sharing about nuisance parameters, not an increase
in the number of treatment assignments.

# Three Layers of Estimation

A useful conceptual decomposition is:

```text
gene-wise counts and fitted means
              ↓
gene-wise dispersion likelihood
              ↓
mean--dispersion trend across genes
              ↓
moderated gene-specific dispersion
```

## Gene-wise likelihood

For fixed fitted means, gene $g$ contributes a likelihood

$$
L_g(\alpha_g)
=\prod_{i=1}^{n}
p_{\mathrm{NB}}(Y_{gi}\mid\mu_{gi},\alpha_g).
$$

Ordinary maximum likelihood for variance components is biased downward in small
samples because regression coefficients were estimated from the same data.
RNA-seq methods therefore use adjustments such as Cox--Reid adjusted profile
likelihood, conditional likelihood, or related bias-reduced procedures. These
improve the starting estimate but do not remove its sampling variability.

## Abundance-dependent trend

Let $\bar\mu_g$ denote a normalized mean abundance and let
$\alpha_{\mathrm{tr}}(\bar\mu_g)$ be a fitted trend. The trend acknowledges that
low-count genes may have a different dispersion distribution from high-count
genes. A parametric, local smooth, or constant trend may be used, but its form
should be checked rather than accepted automatically.

The trend is descriptive across features. It is not a biological law that every
gene must obey. Genes may be unusually variable because of real heterogeneous
regulation, cell-composition changes, mapping ambiguity, outliers, or model
misspecification.

## Moderation toward the trend

On a log-dispersion scale, a schematic empirical-Bayes model is

$$
\log(\alpha_g)\sim
N\!\left(\log\{\alpha_{\mathrm{tr}}(\bar\mu_g)\},\tau^2\right).
$$

Combining this prior with the gene-wise likelihood gives

$$
p(\alpha_g\mid\mathbf y_g)
\propto L_g(\alpha_g)
p(\alpha_g\mid\bar\mu_g,\tau^2).
$$

A posterior mode, posterior mean, or penalized-likelihood solution lies between
the noisy gene-wise estimate and the trend. Weak gene-wise information produces
more shrinkage; many replicates or a sharply peaked likelihood produces less.
The prior scale $\tau$ is learned from the ensemble in empirical Bayes.

This is a bias--variance trade-off. Moderate bias toward a relevant trend can
greatly reduce the variance of gene-wise dispersion estimates and improve the
calibration of many simultaneous tests. If the trend or pooling distribution is
wrong for an important subgroup, shrinkage can instead obscure genuine
heterogeneity.

# DESeq2 and edgeR Use Related, Not Identical, Strategies

DESeq2 first obtains gene-wise dispersion estimates, fits a mean--dispersion
relationship, estimates the spread of log dispersions around it, and forms
maximum-a-posteriori estimates. Genes whose gene-wise dispersion is far above
the fitted distribution can be flagged as dispersion outliers and are not forced
toward the trend in the standard procedure.

edgeR estimates common, trended, and tagwise negative-binomial dispersions using
adjusted profile likelihood and empirical-Bayes moderation. Its prior degrees
of freedom control how strongly tagwise dispersions are squeezed toward the
common or trended value. Robust estimation can reduce the influence of
hypervariable genes when learning the shared distribution.

edgeR's quasi-likelihood pipeline adds a second layer: it estimates quasi-likelihood
dispersions that describe gene-specific uncertainty relative to the negative-binomial
mean--variance relationship. Moderation of these values supports quasi-likelihood
tests with error-rate control that is robust to gene-wise variability.

The numerical dispersions from different packages need not match. Parameterization,
normalization, filtering, design, likelihood adjustment, trend, prior, robust
options, and outlier handling all matter. Method comparison should focus on the
full fitted analysis and inferential calibration, not on whether two stored
columns have identical values.

# Experimental Units and Replication

Suppose treatment is assigned independently to six organoids in each condition,
and each organoid is sequenced in two lanes. The organoids are the experimental
units. Compatible lane counts from the same library may be summed, or a technical
model may retain them, but twelve lanes do not become twelve biological replicates.

Likewise, cells from one specimen, reads from one library, and genes in one assay
are nested or parallel observations. Treating them as independent condition
replicates yields an artificially precise dispersion estimate. If repeated
tissues or time points come from the same donor, donor-level dependence must be
represented by blocking, aggregation, or a suitable repeated-measures method.

The roles of replication are distinct:

| Replicate type | What it can reveal | What it cannot replace |
|---|---|---|
| Independent biological units | population heterogeneity and treatment-effect uncertainty | adequate measurement quality |
| Technical libraries or lanes | assay repeatability and processing failures | additional treatment assignments |
| Reads or fragments | finite counting precision | biological sample-to-sample variation |
| Genes | an ensemble distribution for moderation | biological replication of a condition |

# Design and Normalization Precede Dispersion

The count matrix alone is insufficient. Before estimating dispersions:

1. define the experimental unit and target population;
2. align count columns exactly with sample metadata;
3. construct a full-rank design containing prespecified condition, block, batch,
   and interaction terms needed for the estimand;
4. estimate defensible normalization factors or offsets;
5. filter features using an outcome-independent abundance or prevalence rule;
6. then estimate dispersion conditional on that model.

Normalized counts do not remove batch or donor effects. Scaling factors address
sample-wide measurement scale, whereas design terms describe systematic mean
differences. If treatment is perfectly confounded with batch, no dispersion
procedure can identify a treatment effect separately from the batch effect.

Filtering very weak features can improve estimation because genes with almost
all zero counts contain little information about either mean contrasts or
dispersion. Filtering must not select genes because they already appear to have
large condition differences; that would alter the null distribution of later
tests.

# Diagnostics and Sensitivity

Dispersion shrinkage is not self-validating. Inspect the inputs, the shared trend,
and consequences for inference.

| Question | Diagnostic | Sensitivity or remedy |
|---|---|---|
| Does the trend describe most genes? | gene-wise, fitted, and final dispersion versus mean | compare parametric, local, and constant trends |
| Do a few genes drive the prior? | distribution of residual log dispersions and robust weights | use robust estimation; investigate hypervariable groups |
| Is one sample influential? | count plots, deviance residuals, Cook's distance, library QC | verify metadata; report prespecified exclusion and leave-one-unit-out analyses |
| Is variability condition-specific? | within-group residual spread and BCV plots | consider methods that allow heterogeneous variability or targeted sensitivity analysis |
| Is the design adequate? | design rank, residual degrees of freedom, condition-by-batch table | simplify unsupported questions or collect independent samples |
| Is normalization plausible? | MA plots, size-factor distributions, controls or spike-ins | compare defensible normalization assumptions |

One common failure is allowing true mean differences to masquerade as dispersion.
For example, estimating variability under an intercept-only model when many genes
change by condition attributes systematic signal to noise. The reverse failure
is including data-derived nuisance covariates that remove part of the biology of
interest. Both the mean model and the variance model require scientific judgment.

Important sensitivity analyses repeat the *entire* differential-expression
pipeline under reasonable alternatives: normalization factors, design terms,
trend type, robust moderation, outlier policy, and filtering threshold. Comparing
only the final significant-gene counts hides which estimates changed and why.

# Worked Interpretation

Suppose a gene has fitted normalized mean $\mu=100$ and moderated dispersion
$\widehat\alpha=0.04$. Its model variance at that mean is

$$
100+0.04(100)^2=500,
$$

and its standard deviation is about $22.4$, not the Poisson value $10$. At high
abundance its residual coefficient of variation approaches
$\sqrt{0.04}=0.20$.

Assume the unstable gene-wise estimate was $0.12$ but the abundance trend was
$0.03$. A final estimate of $0.04$ says that the gene-specific likelihood was
not precise enough to support the extreme value against the ensemble pattern.
It does not say that the true dispersion equals $0.04$, that the gene has little
biological importance, or that uncertainty in the dispersion has vanished.

Statistically, the moderated dispersion stabilizes the reference distribution
for the gene's contrast. Biologically, it summarizes unexplained heterogeneity
on the scale and population defined by the study. A high value can reflect real
heterogeneity, technical problems, an omitted mean structure, or a mixture of
these; it is not automatically a quality-control verdict.

# A Minimal Non-executed Workflow

The syntax below is illustrative. It is deliberately not an executable Quarto
cell because this site's publication workflow does not install R or Bioconductor.

```r
# DESeq2 sketch
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
  countData = counts,
  colData = samples,
  design = ~ batch + condition
)
dds <- DESeq(dds, fitType = "parametric")
plotDispEsts(dds)
resultsNames(dds)

# edgeR quasi-likelihood sketch
y <- DGEList(counts)
y <- calcNormFactors(y)
design <- model.matrix(~ batch + condition, data = samples)
y <- estimateDisp(y, design, robust = TRUE)
plotBCV(y)
fit <- glmQLFit(y, design, robust = TRUE)
```

A real analysis must also record sample matching, feature filtering, factor
levels, design rank, package versions, and the exact contrast. Software defaults
are part of the model and should be reported when they affect the result.

- [RNA-seq mean--variance modeling](rna-seq-mean-variance-modeling.qmd) derives
  the negative-binomial variance and precision-weight alternatives.
- [Negative-binomial differential-expression models](negative-binomial-differential-expression-models.qmd)
  develops the count GLM in which dispersion is used.
- [Library-size normalization for RNA-seq](library-size-normalization-for-rna-seq.qmd)
  and [composition bias and normalization factors](composition-bias-and-normalization-factors.qmd)
  explain the offsets that precede dispersion estimation.
- [Shrinkage estimation](../advanced-modeling/shrinkage-estimation.qmd) explains
  the general bias--variance logic of moderation.
- [Biological versus technical replication](biological-versus-technical-replication.qmd)
  defines which observations can inform biological variability.

1. Dispersion is residual variability conditional on normalization, design, and
   the negative-binomial model; it is not a context-free property of a gene.
2. Few biological replicates make gene-wise dispersion estimates unstable even
   when each library contains millions of reads.
3. Mean-dependent trends and empirical-Bayes moderation reduce nuisance-estimation
   variance by borrowing information across genes without treating genes as
   biological replicates.
4. Robustness, outlier handling, and trend checks matter because inappropriate
   pooling can hide real heterogeneity or propagate artifacts.
5. A moderated dispersion calibrates statistical uncertainty; biological meaning
   still depends on experimental units, design, effect size, and validation.
